deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics: no formulas, derivations or computations. It is continuous administrative and scientific prose, the middle part of a formal expert report (Gutachten) addressed to the 'Hohes Curatorium' of the University of Göttingen. The report concerns General Johann Jacob Baeyer's 1861 proposal for a Central European Arc Measurement (Mitteleuropäische Gradmessung) and Hanover's possible part in it.

Content of the page, continuing from 71r:
(1) The previous page argued that a country-wide system of astronomical longitude differences determined by telegraph should be combined with systems of latitude differences and gravity differences (comparative pendulum measurements). Such a combination would let the work surpass similar undertakings in the East and West 'in bedeutender Weise' (the sentence completed at the top of this page).
(2) If all the other Central European states united to fund this extension of the astronomical basis for a more exact determination of the figure of the Earth, Hanover would certainly take a very active part.
(3) If Baeyer's plan were not extended that far, the authors still judge that carrying out this work within Hanover's borders would be possible. Following the hints in the 'Anlage' (appendix), it would also have independent value. That value would not, however, be great enough to justify undertaking it seriously without the prospect of other countries joining.
(4) The authors turn to a second question from the Curatorium. The Curatorium has stated that the intended work should *not* (underlined) lead to a resumption of the triangulation, that is, Gauss's Hanoverian triangulation. The aim is only to draw further scientific conclusions about the figure of the Earth from the existing material, and the Curatorium asks for an opinion on this. The sentence continues on 72r.

The mathematically relevant content is indirect. The proposed combination of triangulation, astronomical latitude and longitude determinations, and gravity (pendulum) determinations is the standard 19th-century programme of physical geodesy. Gravity is used together with arc measurements to determine the geoid or figure of the Earth, in the tradition of Clairaut, Laplace, Gauss, Bessel and Stokes. Any actual theory would be in the 'Anlage' referred to, which is not on this page.

results.what: Recommendation that astronomical longitude and latitude determinations be supplemented by systematic relative gravity (pendulum) measurements to determine the figure of the Earth, within Baeyer's Central European arc measurement
results.modern_name: Physical geodesy programme: combining geometric arc measurement with gravimetry (geoid determination)
results.usually_credited_to: Programme of Baeyer's Mitteleuropäische Gradmessung (1861/62); gravity-figure theory from Clairaut (1743), Laplace, Stokes (1849); later systematised by Helmert (1880-84)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is administrative prose from a Göttingen expert report on Baeyer's Gradmessung proposal. It contains no mathematics. Riemann's possible co-authorship of such a report is a minor biographical detail. The geodetic recommendations themselves (adding pendulum gravity measurements to arc measurements) were standard for the period.

Line 17: 'nicht' in 'wissenschaftlichen Arbeiten nicht zu einer Wiederaufnahme' is underlined in the manuscript; this emphasis should be marked.

Line 1: 'Weise übertragen würden' completes the sentence 'in bedeutender Weise übertragen würden' from the previous page; the image is consistent ('übertroffen' is possible: 'in bedeutender Weise übertroffen würden' fits the sense 'surpassed' better and the letter shapes plausibly).
